Record · Walter Hines Page
A house
directed from London.

Named before it was lived. Built under Ralph Page's supervision. Preserved as the address Page imagined, but never claimed as daily life.

Garran Hill · 1916
Walter Hines Page · 1855–1918
He named it Garran Hill.
The life he imagined happened elsewhere.

In February 1913, Page purchased a thousand-acre farm two miles southwest of Pinehurst, on land his father had logged a generation earlier. He gave it a name before the foundation could answer back: Garran Hill.

Six weeks after buying the land, President Wilson offered him the ambassadorship to the Court of St. James's. Page accepted and sailed for London in May. From three thousand miles away, he directed the making of the house in letters -- asking after the trees, the orchard, the shrubs, the shape of the farm -- while Ralph carried the work on the ground.

"Build the farm, therefore; and let me hear at every stage of that happy game."

He came home in December 1918, carried off the train at Aberdeen on the 11th. His last recorded words at that station: "Well, Frank, I did get here after all, didn't I?" He stayed at Currituck Cottage. Ten days later he was gone. Westminster Abbey placed a memorial tablet. It reads: "The friend of Britain in her sorest need."

"Well, Frank, I did get here after all, didn't I?" — Walter Hines Page, Aberdeen station, December 11, 1918
Architecture · Neo-Georgian

Boston drew the plan.
Pinehurst supplied the hand.

The house does not feel imported because it was never merely installed here. The plans came through a Boston architectural firm; the character came through Pinehurst hands.

Leonard Tufts provided the craftsmen — the same men building the village. They left their evidence in herringbone brick, leaded glass sidelights, arched fanlights, original oak, Delft tile, carved mantels, brass key plates, and a mahogany volute that still turns with the authority of a signature.

This is not ornament trying to prove pedigree. It is pedigree behaving: proportion first, material second, then the confidence to let small survivals carry the authority.

The luxury is not polish. It is proof.

— II — The House
Garran Hill · 1916
The door has been open since 1916.
Inlaid in the threshold brick. Not branding. Not nostalgia. Evidence — laid into the house before anyone knew what the house would outlive.
Restoration Record · 1998–2001

Fourteen quiet years.
Then the house was believed again.

After Betty Dumaine's death, Hollycrest stood vacant for roughly fourteen years — long enough for a lesser house to lose its nerve.

The current stewards purchased the house in 1998 and restored it with the rare discipline of people who understood the assignment: not reinvention, but custody.

The restoration record includes architectural drawings, repaired oak floors, revived details, a kitchen built in the language of the old house, and the crucial refusal to make the place newly clever.

Original

Oak floors, threshold, leaded glass, brass key plates, staircase volute, carved mantels, and the surviving architectural rhythm of 1916.

Restored

Rooms returned to proportion, systems renewed, and details repaired without sanding the soul off the house.

Added Carefully

The kitchen: not original to 1916, but original to the restoration — practical and honest about its date.

The Staircase
The house gives you the stair
before it gives you itself.
Leaded glass sidelights. Arched fanlight above the door. Original oak floors. The mahogany volute turns at the foot of the stair like a signature the house never lost.
The brass key plates on every door still have their original keys.
— III — The Rooms
The Salon
Fire going,
no one home yet.
Nearly forty feet of light and original oak. The Salon is named correctly -- not a living room, never a living room. It understands the difference between a reception and a winter evening. Seven windows. A carved mantel. The room does not ask you to choose between them.
The Drawing Room
They made it bigger
so they could dance.
Someone specified that the coffered ceiling be enlarged so there would be room to dance. Someone else built it exactly that way. The Georgian carved mantel is original. The blue-and-white Delft tile surround is original, hand-painted, one of seven fireplaces in the house.
The room does not feel added to. It feels inevitable.
The Dining Room
Formal by proportion.
Intimate by firelight.
The curved north bay pulls the grounds in through nine-pane divided lights, floor to ceiling. Shell alcoves with scalloped tops flank the fireplace on both sides -- built-in, original, architectural. A chandelier hangs at the center of a room that was designed to make people stay seated longer than they planned to.
It has not stopped doing that.
The Kitchen
The kitchen is not original to 1916.
It is original to the restoration.
Reclaimed heart-pine floors -- the one honest exception in a house of original oak. Two farm sinks. A butler's pantry with its own architectural detail sheet. Sub-Zero. Black-and-white toile. And a wall of windows over the main sink that looks directly onto the magnolias.
The kitchen is not original to 1916. It is original to the restoration. That is why it belongs.
The Library
The room that makes silence
feel inherited.
In a house named by a publisher and built for a man of letters, the library does not feel like an amenity. It feels like a rightful inheritance. Three walls of shelving, floor to ceiling. A rolling ladder. French doors to the rear grounds. The bookshelves had their own full architectural detail sheet in the 1999 restoration record.
Someone drew them on paper before the first shelf was built. That is not decoration. That is authorship.
Powder Room
The Jewel Box
Fuchsia chinoiserie. Tennessee marble vanity.
The size of a secret. The confidence of a full room. Fuchsia chinoiserie wallpaper, Tennessee marble vanity, gilded fixtures, a skirted sink. A powder room that makes people stop walking and say something out loud.
Every house this old earns one room that does exactly what it wants. This is that room.
The Primary Suite
Upstairs, the house stops performing.
It becomes private.
The primary suite had its own full architectural detail sheet -- every panel, every moulding, drawn and specified before a single nail was driven. Four-poster bed, carved fireplace, sitting room, dressing room, a marble bath. The windows pull the grounds up with you.
Privacy here is not absence. It is the house keeping its word.
Primary Bath
Marble, restraint,
and no apology.
The private rooms do not abandon the house's grammar. They quiet it — stone, light, proportion, and enough modern comfort to serve the old structure rather than shout over it.
— IV — The Land
4.15 Acres · Pinehurst, North Carolina
In 1916, those were saplings.
Now they are a forest.
The original farm ran to a thousand acres. What remains is the part Page's son kept as home -- 4.15 acres of camellias, magnolias, dogwoods, American plane trees, and shade that has had a century to become itself. Leonard Tufts' craftsmen built this house. The same hands were building the Carolina Hotel and the Holly Inn. The grounds carry their measure.
Not the whole thousand acres. The part that remembers.
Pool · Grounds
Even the pool knows
how to stay quiet.
A 20-by-40 concrete pool, converted to saltwater in 2022, set into the grounds rather than paraded across them.
— V — Stewardship
Hollycrest · 1959–1984

She renamed it Hollycrest.
Then gave it a second world.

Elizabeth “Betty” Dumaine purchased the house in 1959 and renamed it Hollycrest. The name held long enough to become the address. It is still there, in 200 Hollycrest Drive, even after the house returned to Garran Hill.

At nineteen, Betty attended the Edith Johnson School in Cambridge, Massachusetts, where her roommate was Khun Sangwan Chukramol. The friendship did not stay small. Sangwan later married Prince Mahidol of Songkla and became Srinagarindra, Princess Mother of Thailand.

From Pinehurst, she stayed close to the Princess Mother's work in Northern Thailand -- fundraising, riding, maintaining a friendship that had started at nineteen and lasted a lifetime. She kept horses, hounds, and peacocks. She planted the camellias, the roses, the dogwoods. She gave these grounds their second great life.

Her version of stewardship was not quiet in the small sense. It had peacocks, gardens, horses, charity, ceremony, and one little grave at the back of the grounds that still knows how to break your heart.

Blue Fox · 1946–1969
Someone still
puts flowers there.

At the back of the grounds, beneath a slate cover with a brass marker, Betty Dumaine buried Blue Fox -- her Irish hunter. The horse died in 1969. She was still living here. She put the marker herself.

She has been gone since 1984. The marker remains. Someone still puts flowers there.

Blue Fox — My Irish Hunter — 1946 to 1969.

— VI — The Record
The Record

The record is not thin.

This is not atmosphere. The record holds: Page's letters at Houghton Library. PineStraw's account of the farm. The Village Heritage Foundation's Hollycrest record. TPMCF's biography of Betty Dumaine. NCpedia. The inscription at Westminster Abbey. The threshold brick. Fifteen sets of architectural drawings. The keys still in the plates.

The rare thing is not that the house has a story. The rare thing is that the story still has an address, a threshold, a stair, a key in the plate, and a door that opens.
